message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt for the deposit.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but do so carefully and document everything. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Keep a record of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry and keep a log of visits. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to “quiet enjoyment” of the premises. Landlord cannot harass or interfere with your privacy. | • If you feel your privacy is violated, document incidents and consider contacting local authorities or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the court process: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days) for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, seek legal help immediately. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may repair the issue yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must:
1. Give written notice of the problem.
2. Allow the landlord a reasonable time to fix it.
3. Keep receipts and document the repair. | • Use reputable contractors and keep all invoices. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required, having a written lease protects both parties. | • If you’re renting verbally, ask the landlord to put the agreement in writing. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays which utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Generally requires landlord’s written consent unless the lease allows it. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you may want it to cover personal property and liability. | • Consider a basic policy; many insurers offer short‑term or “short‑term” policies. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division
• Texas Commission on Human Rights
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union)
• Legal Aid services in your county | • Use these resources for disputes, eviction defense, or lease negotiations. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, late fees, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask about security deposit limits** and how it will be returned. 3. **Confirm who pays utilities** and any other recurring costs. 4. **Request a written inventory** of the unit’s condition. 5. **Verify the landlord’s contact information** and emergency procedures. ### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Send a written notice (email or certified mail) detailing the problem and request a repair date. | If no response in 10–14 days, consider filing a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or a local housing agency. | | Unlawful eviction notice | Review the notice for compliance with Texas law. | Contact a tenant‑rights organization or attorney; you may be able to file a defense in court. | | Discrimination claim | Gather evidence (emails, witnesses, photos). | File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, reasonable notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for rent payment and lease termination. Keep detailed records, communicate in writing, and use local resources if you encounter problems.
